items.title: AI opens new era in cognitive studies of wild primates
items.summary: Scientists created an AI system that uses facial recognition and real-time touchscreen testing to automate cognitive studies of capuchin monkeys in the wild. The American Journal of Primatology published a proof-of-concept for the novel method—dubbed CapuchinAI—developed by researchers at Emory Univ

items.title: Možete li spavati po ovim vrućinama?
items.summary: MNOGI oka nisu sklopili po vrućinama koje sve jače pogađaju i Europu. Možda zvuči kao pretjerivanje, ali se zaista spava manje i mnogo lošije. A to je problem i za mentalno i za tjelesno zdravlje.

items.title: Electron cooling tames highly charged ions in Penning trap for first time
items.summary: Researchers at Technical University of Darmstadt and the GSI Helmholtz Center for Heavy Ion Research have succeeded for the first time in decelerating highly charged ions from the GSI accelerator to low energies and subsequently storing them in a Penning trap. items.title: Unusual metal oxide shows signs of magnetism under lattice strain in ultrathin layers
items.summary: Ruthenium dioxide (RuO2) is a metal oxide that commonly serves as an important metallic conductor, quantum material and industrial electrocatalyst. While there have been debates surrounding the magnetic properties of RuO2, it is generally thought to be nonmagnetic in its bulk form. But now, a new st

items.title: Oil droplets remodel themselves, swallow their surroundings like living cells
items.summary: NYU researchers have made microscopic oil droplets in water do something usually reserved for living cells: change shape in complex, controllable ways and even engulf their surroundings.

items.title: Four ways wildfires generate tornadoes, lightning and other extreme weather, sometimes miles from the flames
items.summary: Thick smoke from massive wildfires has been spreading in North America and Europe once again in 2026. The health impacts of breathing this particle-filled air are becoming well known, but wildfires' influence on the weather is less widely recognized.

items.title: Brittany burial mounds may hide human-shaped stones as Coëby cemetery mystery deepens
items.summary: For archaeologists, the Coëby cemetery in Brittany, France, is a gold mine for research. It contains several prehistoric stone monuments and earth mounds. In a new study of two unusually large mounds, scientists may have stumbled upon a rare style of funerary monument.

items.title: Insights into bee biology could ease US rules for organic honey
items.summary: Strict regulations have prevented continental U.S. beekeepers from participating in the lucrative organic honey market, but new research finds that bees' actual habits make certain rules too extreme. The findings potentially provide evidence for federal agencies to ease restrictions and open or

items.title: Moonlight-like fur and feathers may explain Egyptian god Thoth's two animal forms
items.summary: The ancient Egyptian god of the moon had two very different faces: a crescent-beaked white bird and a silver-coated baboon. Now, researchers think they may have found the common thread connecting them all.

items.title: Klima-uređaji nas neće spasiti od vrućine. Znanstvenici nude drugo rješenje
items.summary: DO 2040. između 64 i 100 milijuna kućanstava u četiri velike zemlje moglo bi trebati hlađenje, ali si ga ne bi moglo priuštiti.

items.title: Pacific cloud brightening could weaken El Nino, but models reveal risks for Europe and Asia
items.summary: A brewing "super" El Nino cycle is poised to unleash heat waves, floods and drought worldwide, with the effects amplified by long-term human-caused climate change.

items.title: NASA’s Curiosity rover finds a mysterious honeycomb landscape on Mars
items.summary: NASA’s Curiosity rover has entered a Martian valley covered by an astonishing “sea” of tiny polygon-shaped fractures. The honeycomb patterns, each only a few inches wide, stretch across the landscape and even wrap around a nearby 20-foot-tall butte.

items.title: Tiny black holes may be secretly exploding stars across the Milky Way
items.summary: Primordial black holes may occasionally pass through white dwarf stars and trigger enormous Type Ia supernova explosions. Researchers found that these events could explain chemical patterns seen in supernova remnants, nearby explosions, and stars across the Milky Way.

items.title: Researchers investigate case of soft-tick borne relapsing fever in Austin area
items.summary: Researchers at Baylor College of Medicine and the Texas Department of State Health Services have reported a likely case of soft tick-borne relapsing fever (STRF) in an Austin-area resident. Now, they highlight the growing risk of exposure to infected ticks in urban and residential settings. The stud

items.title: Ant brains reveal how evolution turned hunger into parenting
items.summary: Ant parenting may have evolved from the same brain systems that once controlled hunger. Researchers found that two chemical signals push clonal raider ants toward either caring for larvae or leaving to forage, with the balance changing as the ants grow older. Similar signals are involved in mammalia

items.title: New immune-blocking strategy improves interspecies organ generation
items.summary: Xenophagocytosis is a natural immune process that limits interspecies organ generation by eliminating living donor cells, researchers at the Institute of Science Tokyo, Japan, report. By uncovering how embryonic macrophages eliminate living donor cells, the researchers developed strategies to block

items.title: Eating one avocado a day may lower heart disease risk
items.summary: A daily avocado may help lower heart disease risk in adults with obesity by reducing the number of LDL particles circulating in the blood. After six months, participants who ate an avocado each day experienced a decline associated with an estimated 4% reduction in cardiovascular risk.

items.title: Scientists may have found a way to prevent statin muscle pain
items.summary: Scientists have identified an immune response that may explain why statins cause muscle pain, weakness, and exercise intolerance in some people. The finding could eventually lead to treatments that protect muscles while preserving the drugs’ lifesaving cardiovascular benefits.

items.title: Sensor-embedded 3D-printed repairs could help preserve ancient pottery
items.summary: Koç University researchers have developed a conservation method that combines photogrammetry, digital modeling, 3D printing and embedded sensors to replace missing sections of archaeological amphorae. The customized fills can also monitor environmental and physical changes affecting the artifacts, o

items.title: Quantum computer completes verified task beyond practical reach of classical simulations
items.summary: IBM and researchers from the University of Chicago announced a demonstration in quantum computing that meets the fundamental criteria for "quantum advantage"—the point where quantum computers can be confirmed to have outperformed classical computers on trusted computations.

items.title: Ancient diamond preserves evidence of water-bearing mineral deep in Earth's mantle
items.summary: A team of Brazilian researchers discovered the first direct evidence that goethite—the mineral responsible for the brown color of soils—can withstand extreme pressures and temperatures all the way to the planet's interior inside a diamond just 3 millimeters (0.1 inch) long, within a microscopic

items.title: Deadly blooms offer a genetic blueprint for making hard-to-synthesize medicinal compounds
items.summary: Two plants that cause neurotoxicity and paralysis in the tiniest doses are also known to counter pain, malaria, cancer and pests. For the first time, researchers discovered a way to recreate these powerful compounds in the lab, helping lead the way to improved, naturally sourced therapeutics.

items.title: Leave it: Dog trainers help pets avoid poisonous snakes
items.summary: Ripley, a medium-sized dog with a strong prey drive, curiously approached Brian, a large western diamondback rattlesnake, until she got a quick zap on the neck meant to simulate a venomous viper's bite.

items.title: Scientists left water inside a battery and nearly doubled its power
items.summary: A surprisingly simple change could make sodium-ion batteries far more powerful while opening the door to turning seawater into drinking water. Researchers at the University of Surrey found that sodium vanadium oxide performs much better when its naturally occurring water is left inside instead of be

items.title: Solar wind stirs Mars' upper atmosphere, boosting ion loss to space
items.summary: Our sun constantly releases a stream of high-speed charged particles, known as the solar wind. Unlike Earth, Mars does not have a strong global magnetic field to shield its atmosphere from this flow. items.title: A rollercoaster of weather extremes: Drought and heat waves are creating UK's climate whiplash
items.summary: The UK is bouncing from one type of extreme weather to another this year. This is climate whiplash. Caused by changes in the fast-moving body of air high in the atmosphere called the jet stream, climate whiplash has become more likely with climate change. items.title: Strengthening El Nino 'adding fuel to a planet already on fire': UN chief
items.summary: A strengthening El Niño that could shatter all-time records is "adding fuel to a planet already on fire" and pushing the world into "uncharted territory," U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned Friday.

items.title: Hungary to shut nuclear plant as heatwave hits central Europe
items.summary: Hungary's sole nuclear power plant will be shut down next week because of low water levels in the Danube, Prime Minister Peter Magyar said Friday as central Europe slogs through the latest in a series of heat waves.

items.title: Superheated magma may power towering lava fountains
items.summary: Scientists studying magma from the 2021 Tajogaite eruption on La Palma have discovered that extreme heat can dramatically change how an eruption unfolds. items.title: Scientists found two mysterious ‘ghost’ ancestors hiding in our DNA
items.summary: Modern humans carry DNA from two mysterious extinct lineages in addition to Neanderthals and Denisovans. Their hidden genetic legacy shows that our evolutionary past was shaped by repeated mixing among many different human groups.

items.title: What’s Up: August 2026 Skywatching Tips from NASA
items.summary: A solar eclipse, the Perseids, bright Venus after sunset, and a deep partial lunar eclipse highlight August’s skywatching. Skywatching Highlights Transcript A solar eclipse, one of the year’s best meteor showers, Venus at its brightest in the evening sky, and a lunar eclipse to close out the month.

items.title: Fish pathogens once limited to Asia and US emerge in Brazilian farms
items.summary: For the first time in Brazil, scientists have identified the presence of bacteria that cause columnaris disease, a serious disease in farmed fish intended for human consumption. items.title: Moonquakes could reveal ice buried beneath lunar south polar craters
items.summary: Finding water on the moon may only be a matter of detecting the right vibrations.

items.title: Laying odds on the potential for Martian water near future landing zones
items.summary: We know Mars has water ice in its polar regions, but astronauts (and their solar-powered equipment!) would much rather experience life closer to Mars' equator. items.title: Art festivals may revive island communities when tourism stays within local limits
items.summary: Grounding intermittent art festivals such as the Setouchi Triennale within the resource capacities and social thresholds of the island communities that host them is a path to the sustainable, long-term revitalization of these communities.

items.title: NASA to Host Florida Event Celebrating American Air, Space Leadership
items.summary: NASA will hold a news conference at 2:30 p.m. EDT, Friday, Aug. 14, live from the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, and media and digital creators are invited to attend in person. items.title: Smarter fish farms could cut electricity use and CO₂ while keeping fish safe
items.summary: Recirculating aquaculture systems (RAS) are attracting growing attention as a sustainable aquaculture technology that can reduce water use, control rearing conditions and lower environmental impacts by filtering and reusing water. items.title: A new genetic tool helps researchers uncover the logic of gene regulation
items.summary: The human genome contains more than 20,000 genes. However, at any given time and in a given cell, only a fraction are active. Researchers from EMBL Heidelberg's Krebs Group have developed an innovative experimental approach to understand how cells determine which genes to turn on and when.

items.title: From research to policy: Study turns EU wildfire assessments into a tool for better governance
items.summary: Climate change, land-use change and socioeconomic pressures are turning wildfires from a primarily ecological process into a complex, systemic risk that cuts across ecosystems, infrastructure, public health, water resources, cultural heritage and rural livelihoods. items.title: Newly discovered mechanism protects DNA during cell division
items.summary: Every time a cell divides, it must accurately copy and distribute its DNA between two new cells. However, in some cases, chromosomes do not fully separate, leaving behind thin strands of DNA known as DNA bridges that connect the two newly formed cells.

items.title: Isotopic analysis may help police combat illegal timber trade in Amazon
items.summary: A map showing the distribution of isotopes in Amazonian tree wood can help identify illegally harvested timber. items.title: Homing in on the X-ray sky with eROSITA's second data release
items.summary: The German eROSITA consortium (eROSITA-DE), which includes the University of Bonn and is led by the Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics (MPE), has released its second major public data set, the "eROSITA Data Release 2" (DR2).

items.title: NASA’s Newest Wind Tunnel Opens at NASA Langley
items.summary: On Friday, July 31, 2026, NASA leadership and Virginia government officials opened NASA’s first major new wind tunnel in more than 40 years, the Flight Dynamics Research Facility at NASA’s Langley Research Center in Hampton, Virginia.
